stem: A delivery driver operates a box truck with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,001 lb across a state line. Which statement is correct?
options: The vehicle is a commercial motor vehicle and the driver needs a DOT medical certificate
The vehicle is under the 26,001-lb threshold, so no DOT physical is required
The driver needs a DOT physical only if the truck is placarded for hazardous materials
The driver needs a CDL and a DOT physical
explanation: A CMV in interstate commerce is any vehicle with a GVWR/GCWR (or actual weight, whichever is greater) of 10,001 lb or more, so this driver must be medically certified. 26,001 lb is the CDL threshold, not the CMV threshold; hazmat placarding is a separate, independent trigger; and a 10,001-lb truck does not by itself require a CDL.

stem: A driver reads 20/40 with the right eye, 20/50 with the left eye, and 20/30 with both eyes together, all with glasses. Under the standard vision requirement he:
options: Qualifies for 1 year with periodic monitoring
Does not meet the standard, because each eye must reach 20/40
Qualifies if a road test is passed
explanation: The standard requires distant acuity of at least 20/40 in EACH eye and 20/40 with both eyes, with or without corrective lenses. A 20/50 eye fails, and there is no short certificate or road test that cures it — the driver's route is the Alternative Vision Standard of 391.44.

options: At least 70° in the horizontal meridian in each eye
At least 85° in the horizontal meridian in the better eye
At least 70° in the better eye only
explanation: Each eye must have a field of vision of at least 70° in the horizontal meridian. A 55° eye fails and should be referred; a driver with one failing eye may pursue the Alternative Vision Standard.

stem: How is the forced-whisper test performed and passed?
options: Whisper at 10 ft in a quiet room; the driver must pass with both ears
Whisper at 5 ft using residual breath after a normal exhalation, one ear at a time, out of the driver's line of sight; the better ear must perceive the whisper
Whisper at 5 ft while the driver watches your lips; either ear may pass
Whisper at 3 ft; both ears must pass
explanation: Stand 5 ft from the ear being tested, out of the line of sight so lips cannot be read, occlude the other ear, and whisper random words, letters, and numbers using only the breath remaining after a normal expiration. The standard is met if a forced whisper is first perceived at not less than 5 ft in the better ear.

stem: Audiometry shows an average loss of 32.7 dB in the right ear and 46 dB in the left ear at 500, 1,000, and 2,000 Hz. The driver:
options: Fails, because one ear exceeds 40 dB
Fails, because the two-ear average exceeds 40 dB
Passes, because the better ear averages 40 dB or less
explanation: The audiometric standard is an average hearing loss of no more than 40 dB at 500, 1,000, and 2,000 Hz in the better ear, with or without a hearing aid. Only the better ear has to pass; 3,000 Hz is not part of the standard.

stem: An outside audiology report gives thresholds calibrated to ISO rather than ANSI Z24.5-1951. How do you convert before averaging?
options: Subtract 14, 10, and 8.5 dB at 500, 1,000, and 2,000 Hz
explanation: The regulation specifies an audiometer calibrated to ANSI Z24.5-1951. ISO values read higher, so subtract 14 dB at 500 Hz, 10 dB at 1,000 Hz, and 8.5 dB at 2,000 Hz to convert, then average the three ANSI values for each ear.

stem: A driver meets the hearing standard only while wearing his hearing aid. Which is correct?

He may be certified for only 1 year
He needs a federal hearing exemption
He is disqualified because the standard must be met unaided
explanation: Both hearing tests may be met with or without a hearing aid. A driver who qualifies with the aid must wear it and keep it operating while driving; the certificate is marked accordingly and can run the full 2 years. stem: A driver arrives wearing a hearing aid but says he barely needs it. What is the recommended testing sequence?
options: Test without the aid first; test with the aid only if he fails unaided
Skip the whisper test and go straight to audiometry
Require an audiologist's report before testing
explanation: The 2024 Handbook does not prescribe a testing order — it says only that a driver with a hearing aid or cochlear implant can be qualified as long as the standard is met, with or without the aid, and that a driver who fails the whisper test in both ears goes on to audiometry. A driver who passes unaided takes no 'wearing hearing aid' restriction. The better-ear rule applies either way — 3 ft unaided in one ear and 5 ft aided in the other meets the standard with the aid.

explanation: The standard bars a mental, nervous, organic, or functional disease or psychiatric disorder LIKELY TO INTERFERE with safe driving. Diagnosis alone never disqualifies — the examiner judges function: can the driver appreciate, evaluate, and respond to stress?

stem: Under the traditional FMCSA psychiatric tables, a driver treated for a non-psychotic major depressive episode without suicidal behavior may be considered for certification after:
explanation: Traditional benchmark: 6 months symptom-free for a non-psychotic major depression without suicidal behavior. A severe episode, a suicide attempt, or a manic episode traditionally waits 1 year. The maximum certificate in these cases is 1 year, with evaluation by a mental-health professional familiar with CMV driving. options: Is disqualified because lithium is a controlled substance
May be certified — lithium has little evidence of impairing driving when levels are therapeutic and the driver is asymptomatic
Must switch to another mood stabilizer
explanation: Lithium is not a controlled substance and has little evidence of driving impairment. Certification depends on the driver being asymptomatic with levels in the therapeutic range and the underlying disorder stable.

stem: Under the traditional guidance, which sedative-hypnotic prescription is compatible with certification?
options: A short-acting agent (half-life under 5 hours), at the lowest dose, for less than 2 weeks
Any agent if prescribed by a psychiatrist
explanation: Only a short-acting sedative-hypnotic (half-life under 5 hours), at the lowest effective dose, for under 2 weeks — or a non-sedating anxiolytic — is compatible. Diazepam's half-life is 24–48 hours (five half-lives to clear), and the first question is always why it was prescribed: diazepam for alcohol withdrawal implies current alcoholism, which is disqualifying.

options: Disqualify — Schedule II drugs are incompatible with driving
Apply the prescription exception: obtain the prescriber's evaluation (the optional MCSA-5895), verify the diagnosis, and assess side effects before deciding
explanation: Stimulants are controlled substances but not Schedule I, so 391.41(b)(12)(ii) applies: a prescription from a licensed practitioner familiar with the driver's history and duties who advises the drug will not affect safe driving. stem: Compared with SSRIs, first-generation tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, clomipramine, amoxapine) are of concern to the examiner because they:

explanation: TCAs are sedating and impair alertness; the traditional (pre-2024) therapy tables advised against certifying drivers on first-generation antidepressants, and today they are assessed individually. stem: A driver uses CBD gummies labeled 'less than 0.3% THC.' The most accurate counseling is:
options: CBD is Schedule I; he is disqualified
CBD under 0.3% THC is not marijuana under federal law, but products are unregulated and may contain enough THC to produce a positive, disqualifying DOT drug test
CBD is fully safe and never tests positive
explanation: Hemp-derived CBD with under 0.3% THC is not a controlled substance, but there is no federal labeling oversight; DOT's Office of Drug and Alcohol Policy warns that CBD use can produce a positive THC test, which is not a legitimate medical explanation. Discuss the risk.

options: Methadone does not automatically preclude certification; obtain the prescriber's information that treatment will not affect safe driving, then decide
He may be certified only if switched to buprenorphine

explanation: Older advisory language listed methadone as disqualifying; the 2024 Handbook removed that reference. Methadone (Schedule II) and buprenorphine (Schedule III) are handled under the prescription exception with prescriber input, and the examiner makes the final determination.

It is the motor carrier's program under 49 CFR Parts 382 and 40 and tests for marijuana, cocaine, amphetamines, opioids, and phencyclidine — not alcohol
It is part of the required urinalysis on the MER
A Substance Abuse Professional must review every result

stem: On exam a driver has dilated pupils, tachycardia, cool moist skin, and gives a vague history. The examiner:
options: Must arrange a DOT 5-panel test through the employer
May order a non-DOT drug test and, if the driver refuses and current use cannot be excluded, may disqualify
Cannot test without a Substance Abuse Professional
Must certify if the driver denies use
explanation: The examiner may order a non-DOT test when the history or exam suggests use; no SAP is involved. A driver who refuses and in whom current use cannot be ruled out is not certified, and fresh needle tracks are not certified either.

stem: A driver answers 'yes' to two CAGE questions. What does this score mean and what is the next step?
options: A score of 2 or more suggests alcohol dependence; consider a non-DOT alcohol test and further evaluation, with the diagnosis being the examiner's call
Referral to a Substance Abuse Professional is mandatory
explanation: CAGE (Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener) of 2 or more, or an AUDIT score of 8 or more, is a positive screen. Neither instrument is mandated by FMCSA; a positive screen prompts further evaluation and the examiner decides whether a current clinical diagnosis of alcoholism exists.

stem: A driver's medication list includes disulfiram (Antabuse). The most important implication for certification is:
options: None — disulfiram is not a controlled substance
It implies a current clinical diagnosis of alcoholism, which precludes certification under 391.41(b)(13)
explanation: Disulfiram is prescribed to deter drinking in a driver being treated for alcoholism — i.e., a condition not yet stabilized. A current clinical diagnosis of alcoholism precludes certification, just as diazepam prescribed for alcohol withdrawal does.

stem: A driver was treated for alcoholism 10 years ago, has completed treatment, has been sober since, and has no residual impairment. He:
options: Is disqualified — a history of alcoholism is permanent
May be certified, for up to 2 years, because 'current' means active illness or a condition not yet stabilized
May be certified for 1 year only
Needs a Substance Abuse Professional's clearance
explanation: The standard is no CURRENT clinical diagnosis of alcoholism. A driver in sustained remission with treatment completed and no residual impairment may be certified, up to 2 years. Alcohol-related complications such as alcoholic neuropathy are judged under their own standard, (b)(7).

stem: Alprazolam, diazepam, zolpidem, and tramadol belong to which DEA schedule?
explanation: Benzodiazepines, zolpidem, tramadol, and modafinil are Schedule IV (limited dependence potential). Schedule II holds the 'dangerous' drugs — stimulants such as amphetamine salts and lisdexamfetamine, and opioids such as oxycodone, fentanyl, and methadone. Schedule III includes acetaminophen-codeine (Tylenol #3), buprenorphine, testosterone, and ketamine; Schedule V includes pregabalin and diphenoxylate-atropine.
